why: No halting condition is known at all. The wall update depends only on the wall and N mod 2, so a closed set of walls for both parities would prove non-halting with no number theory. New here: the stack-of-counters model matches the Lean step map on all 558 steps of the free-parity wall graph to 300 cells. Under free parities no count goes below zero (29,195 walls to 30,000 cells), counters below the top never pass 17, and each counter is at least 5 times the one below it. Along the real orbit (300,000 steps) the counters below the top stay at 10 or less. A count can go negative only if the counter above stays odd for as many steps as its own size, which is a 2-adic coincidence. The reachable walls get at most 10% of the way there.
next: Prove an invariant on the stack (each counter far above the one below), then the stack rules in Lean.

why: It halts only if every run of 1s is even at once, so the whole stack has to empty. An invariant that keeps one run odd would settle it. The parity of the number of even runs is already known, so a parity-type invariant is plausible.
next: Search for an invariant on run parities, using the Lean visit map.

why: It halts only at b = 1 with a = 0 mod 4. The map is fully proved for even a, but b only drops by subtraction steps, which mix residues.
next: Prove the halting events in Lean (only simulated so far), then look for an invariant on (a mod 4, b).

why: New here: this machine and the next two iterate the same function n -> 3n - 10*2^k + 3k + 14 (k the level, h_k = 5*2^k - k - 6). Starts are 4, 10 and 1, and the orbits are disjoint for the first 20,000 steps. Halting means landing exactly on h_k.
next: Done here: lean/Closed.lean proves the closed form for every n (kernel). What is left is the hitting question: does the orbit ever land on some h_k?

why: Same doubling pass (a,b) -> (2a+2, b-2a-2). It halts if a pass ends with b = 0, and the chance of that falls with the width.
It halts iff a doubling chain meets x = (m+7)(2^(k+1)-1)/2 - k - 1. The total chance of a hit is 0.3187, nearly all of it in the first 20 rounds, but the chain-end remainders cover all of [0, h).
next: Prove the chain criterion in Lean (an induction on k).

why: Non-halting is reduced to the orbit staying out of a small uncovered region (Z_k with k = 0 or n < 12k+12). n has thousands of digits, so a growth bound k <= f(n) would be enough, but k follows its own 3/2 rule.
next: Prove the uncovered Z_k cases, then try a growth bound on k.

why: It halts iff the orbit of 44 lands on 2^(j+1) - 2j - 7 or on a restart with d + s + 4 = 2^(s+2). There is about one target per doubling band, and t grows about 1.3x per reset.
next: A last-step congruence lemma, in the style of the Doucette family's Preimage.lean.

why: It halts iff a Y run starts with c - b = 3, which parity rules out during the doubling stage. Outside that stage the chance is about 1/N per run.
next: A closed form for the end of a round.

why: It halts at a reset with 2u = v exactly. Reset k needs about 1.47^k operations, so resets are rare.
A round halts only when a block is a base-6 repunit-like number. The chance is about 6^-D per round for D-digit blocks.
next: A digit automaton for the block, if its updates are digit-local.

why: After the first round c = 0 mod 3, but a mod 3 mixes. A residue search with branch guards relaxed (residues.py) reaches the halting difference for every modulus 2^a 3^b up to 7,776.
It halts iff r = p + 1, which is a divisibility condition P(2^(t+1) - 1) = r + t + 1 at the end of each doubling phase. residues.py finds the halting class for every modulus 2^a 3^b up to 7,776.
Subtract the smaller and triple it. It halts at u - v in {0, 1}, with a chance of about 2^-size per round. Residues mix (residues.py).
